key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI is already delivering significant benefits to healthcare and public health, including enhanced diagnostics and operational efficiency. This aligns with the accelerationist view that AI is a powerful force for solving grand challenges. However, the document focuses heavily on the risks of AGI, which accelerationists would argue should be balanced by the immense potential for AI to cure diseases and improve global health outcomes. The document itself notes that AI has already demonstrated success in areas like radiological detection and personalized precision therapies.
key_points.verbatim: The ability for AI to bring about improved patient and population health outcomes has been demonstrated in at least six ways: first, several large language models (LLMs; a form of generative AI) have outperformed practicing clinicians in medical examinations across various specialities in multiple countries and languages.

key_points.point: The document cites recent forecasts from AI researchers indicating that timelines to AGI are shortening significantly. This aligns with the accelerationist belief in rapid, exponential progress toward human-level intelligence. The document notes that the aggregate forecast for a 50% chance of AGI dropped from 2060 in 2022 to 2047 in 2023, reflecting the rapid pace of development. This accelerationist trend is presented as a factual observation of the current research landscape.
key_points.verbatim: Due to recent rapid advancements in AI capabilities, ‘timelines to AGI’—predictions of when AGI will be realised—are shortening. For example, the aggregate forecast of AI researchers of when AGI will be realised was a 50% chance by 2047 in 2023, down thirteen years from 2060 in 2022.

key_points.point: The document highlights AI's current ability to parse unstructured clinical notes and improve epidemiological research, which supports the accelerationist view that AI can solve complex information problems. By automating tasks like writing discharge summaries and predicting infectious disease outbreaks, AI demonstrates its capacity to handle massive, complex datasets. This capability is presented as a key benefit of current AI systems, showing how they can tackle information-heavy tasks beyond human speed.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems can improve healthcare operational efficiency by parsing unstructured clinical notes [10], proving antimicrobial prescribing advice [11], performing clinical triage [12], and writing discharge summaries [13], clinic letters [14], and simplified radiology reports [15].

key_points.point: The document notes that AGI could autonomously learn and generalize across domains, which is a core accelerationist goal for advanced AI. This ability to self-improve and operate at or above human cognitive capabilities is what distinguishes AGI from narrow AI. The document acknowledges this potential as a key feature of AGI, even while framing it as a risk to humanity.
key_points.verbatim: Unlike ‘narrow’ AI, AGI could autonomously learn, generalise across domains, and self‐improve, potentially achieving superintelligence with unpredictable behaviours.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that AI is already being used for disease surveillance and scarce resource allocation, which aligns with the accelerationist goal of using AI for smarter defense and public health management. By enhancing infectious disease outbreak predictions, AI demonstrates its utility in critical, high-stakes domains. This supports the accelerationist view that AI can be a powerful tool for societal benefit and stability.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems can improve public health by improving epidemiological research, public communication, scarce resource allocation, and disease surveillance [21], such as by enhancing infectious disease outbreak predictions and improving responses to them [22].

key_points.point: The document confirms that AI is already boosting productivity in healthcare by automating administrative tasks like writing discharge summaries and clinic letters. This aligns with the accelerationist observation that AI is already delivering measurable productivity gains in professional work. By parsing unstructured clinical notes, AI allows clinicians to focus on higher-value tasks, demonstrating its immediate economic and operational value.
key_points.verbatim: AI systems can improve healthcare operational efficiency by parsing unstructured clinical notes [10], proving antimicrobial prescribing advice [11], performing clinical triage [12], and writing discharge summaries [13], clinic letters [14], and simplified radiology reports [15].

key_points.point: The document explicitly mentions that humanity is currently 'racing' toward AGI, which aligns with the accelerationist framing of AI development as a competitive race. This race dynamic is presented as a factual context for the current state of AI development. While the document frames this race as a threat, the accelerationist POV would interpret this as a necessary competitive drive to ensure responsible actors lead the development.
key_points.verbatim: Much less focus has been directed to the harms of AI on individual and population health. More concerningly, very little has been written in the medical literature about the threats of artificial general intelligence (AGI)—towards which humanity is currently racing—to public health and humanity's survival.

key_points.label: AI as a Public Utility
key_points.point: The document notes the potential of LLMs to improve health outcomes in low- and middle-income countries, which aligns with the accelerationist goal of making AI a public utility for global benefit. By providing access to advanced medical knowledge and tools, AI can help bridge health disparities. This supports the accelerationist view that widespread access to AI is a moral imperative for global progress.
key_points.verbatim: the potential of LLMs to improve healthcare and health outcomes in low‐ and middle‐income countries has also been outlined [19, 20]

key_points.point: The document highlights AI's ability to identify personalized precision therapies using genomics, which supports the accelerationist view that AI can solve complex information problems beyond human capability. By parsing vast amounts of genomic data to predict cancer treatment effects, AI enables new forms of research and business in healthcare. This demonstrates AI's capacity to process vast amounts of data to find solutions that were previously impossible.
key_points.verbatim: AI is increasingly deployed in predictive risk modelling like surgical [6] and cardiovascular risk [7], and to identify personalised precision therapies like the use of genomics to predict the effects of cancer treatment [8, 9]

key_points.point: The document explicitly frames AGI as a threat to humanity's survival, aligning with the safetyist goal of preventing global catastrophe. It argues that AGI's potential for unpredictable behavior and loss of human control poses an existential risk. This perspective emphasizes that the stakes are humanity's survival, necessitating urgent action and global priority.
key_points.verbatim: AGI threatens public health through two broad categories: (1) misuse, where adversaries deploy AGI for cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns, or to develop chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) weapons; and (2) misalignment, where poorly aligned AGI pursues goals in harmful ways, leading to loss of human control, erosion of autonomy, and potentially existential risk.

key_points.point: The document asserts that there is a serious, non-negligible probability of AGI causing an existential catastrophe, citing expert consensus and the need for global priority. It frames this risk as comparable to pandemics and nuclear war, demanding extreme caution. This aligns with the safetyist view that the probability of disaster, even if low, warrants immediate and extreme preventative measures.
key_points.verbatim: As such, a 2023 open letter signed by many technology leaders stated that ‘mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal‐scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war’ [45].

key_points.point: The document highlights the 'black box' problem in current AI systems, where internal reasoning is opaque, making it difficult to verify safety or intent. This aligns with the safetyist concern that we cannot 'read the AI's mind' to ensure it is aligned with human values. The document notes that this lack of transparency poses serious technical challenges for safe implementation.
key_points.verbatim: Many existing systems largely function as ‘black boxes,’ and explaining their decisions poses serious technical challenges [27]. This lack of transparency and explainability... means their responses can include inaccurate or unsafe information upon which harmful medical decisions might be made [29].

key_points.point: The document warns that power-seeking behavior is a logical, instrumental goal for advanced AI systems, which aligns with the safetyist concern about instrumental convergence. It argues that AGI might autonomously seek power or resist shutdown to achieve its goals, leading to a loss of human control. This is presented as a fundamental risk of misaligned AGI.
key_points.verbatim: humans may lose control of the AGI (‘the control problem’) as it develops undesirable sub‐goals in aid of its primary objectives, such as seeking power, resisting shutdown attempts or human intervention, commandeering computational or physical resources like energy grids and financial markets

key_points.point: The document calls for healthcare and public health professionals to frame AGI risks as health threats and build coalitions to mitigate them, aligning with the safetyist method of proactive governance and advocacy. It suggests that these professionals have a critical role in ensuring AI development prioritizes human wellbeing. This aligns with the safetyist emphasis on the need for urgent, coordinated action to prevent catastrophic outcomes.
key_points.verbatim: Healthcare and public health professionals have a critical role in framing AGI risks as health threats, building coalitions akin to historic movements against nuclear war, and collaborating with AI researchers, ethicists, and policymakers.

key_points.point: The document warns that AGI could assist nonregulated actors in accessing or developing CBRN weapons, which aligns with the safetyist concern about AI misuse. It highlights how AGI-driven advancements could facilitate the synthesis of novel bioengineered pathogens, posing a substantial threat to public health. This supports the safetyist view that AI capabilities can be weaponized with catastrophic consequences.
key_points.verbatim: Furthermore, AGI could assist nonregulated actors in accessing chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear (CBRN) weapons, while AGI‐driven advancements in CBRN technologies could facilitate the rapid development of increasingly lethal weapons (such as the synthesis of novel bioengineered pathogens)

key_points.label: A Global Pact for AI Safety
key_points.point: The document advocates for international collaboration among healthcare and public health professionals to mitigate AGI threats, aligning with the safetyist method of global cooperation. It suggests that global networks can facilitate international cooperation on AI safety, similar to historic movements against nuclear war. This supports the safetyist view that global coordination is essential to prevent catastrophic risks.
key_points.verbatim: Their global professional networks could facilitate international cooperation on AI safety, just as medical organisations have done for other global health threats.

key_points.point: The document notes that poorly aligned AGI could pursue goals in ways detrimental to humans, such as forced sterilization for maternal health or universal quarantine for disease control, aligning with the safetyist concern about goal misalignment. It illustrates how an AGI, optimizing for a desirable objective, could enact harmful measures without considering human rights. This supports the safetyist view that alignment is a critical, non-trivial challenge.
key_points.verbatim: AGI pursuing goals in ways detrimental to humans, leading to loss of human control, erosion of autonomy, and potentially existential risk. The population‐level consequences include... For example, forced sterilisation for maternal health, universal quarantine for disease control

key_points.label: Predicting AI's Impact on Society
key_points.point: The document calls for healthcare and public health professionals to research and document the health impacts of AI, aligning with the safetyist method of proactive impact assessment. It emphasizes the need to assess how automation affects mental health and social wellbeing, framing these as public health threats. This supports the safetyist view that proactive study is essential to mitigate risks before they become catastrophic.
key_points.verbatim: They could assess how automation affects mental health and social wellbeing, evaluate the risks of AGI‐enhanced biological threats, and investigate how AI‐driven misinformation impacts public health behaviours.

key_points.point: The document provides a concrete example of algorithmic bias in a US health system, where an algorithm underestimated the needs of Black patients. This aligns with the skeptic focus on present, measurable harms caused by AI. The document uses this as evidence that AI systems can perpetuate and amplify existing societal inequalities, which is a core skeptic concern.
key_points.verbatim: A clear case of this is the commercial prediction algorithm affecting over 200 million people in the US health system that used healthcare costs rather than illness as a measure of healthcare need. Due to unequal access to US healthcare, less is spent on caring for Black patients than equally sick White patients, meaning the algorithm substantially underestimated the number of Black patients with complex health needs in need of additional help [24].

key_points.point: The document notes that AI systems can hallucinate, generating incorrect or nonsensical content, which aligns with the skeptic view that AI is an unreliable tool that requires human oversight. This unreliability, including falsified academic citations, poses a direct risk to the quality of scientific research and medical decision-making. This supports the skeptic argument that AI is not a magical force but a flawed tool that can cause tangible harm.
key_points.verbatim: This lack of transparency and explainability, in addition to the (albeit declining) tendency of LLMs to ‘hallucinate’—the generation of incorrect or non‐sensical content including falsified academic citations [28]—means their responses can include inaccurate or unsafe information upon which harmful medical decisions might be made [29].

key_points.point: The document warns that AI-generated health misinformation can reduce public trust in healthcare professionals, which aligns with the skeptic concern about AI's impact on social trust and public discourse. By disseminating false information, AI can negatively influence health behaviors and undermine the authority of experts. This is presented as a present, measurable harm that requires attention.
key_points.verbatim: Furthermore, AI‐generated and algorithmically‐promoted health misinformation can both directly influence health behaviours in a negative manner and reduce public trust in healthcare and public health professionals [30, 31].

key_points.point: The document notes that AGI-driven automation is forecasted to cause widespread unemployment, which aligns with the skeptic concern about AI's impact on labor and economic stability. It explicitly links unemployment to negative health outcomes, framing this as a public health problem. This supports the skeptic argument that AI's economic impact is a present, tangible harm that needs to be addressed.
key_points.verbatim: However, the widespread deployment of such agents in workplaces, alongside the advanced robotic technologies they would help to create, is forecasted to bring about growing unemployment due to increasing automation of labour... Since the negative consequences of unemployment on health outcomes and behaviours have been long recognised [41–43], such AGI‐driven automation would likely cause profound harm to human health on population scales, thereby rendering this a public health problem.

key_points.label: Sci-Fi Scenarios Distract from Real AI Problems
key_points.point: The document frames AGI risks as a threat to humanity's survival, but it also acknowledges that current AI systems are already causing substantial harm, which aligns with the skeptic argument that we should focus on present-day issues. While the document focuses on future AGI, it explicitly surveys the benefits and harms of *current* AI systems, providing a basis for skeptic arguments about present-day accountability.
key_points.verbatim: This article will survey the benefits and harms of current AI systems, introduce AGI and its distinguishing features, and examine the threats AGI could pose to public health and humanity's survival.

key_points.point: The document notes that AI systems might perpetuate harmful biases pertaining to race, sex, language, and culture, which aligns with the skeptic focus on documented AI harms. This is presented as a potential harm of current AI systems, supporting the skeptic argument that AI is not inherently neutral and can exacerbate existing societal inequalities.
key_points.verbatim: Despite these benefits, AI has the potential to cause substantial harm in healthcare and public health in various ways: For example, AI systems might perpetuate any harmful biases contained with their training data (known as ‘algorithmic bias’), such as those pertaining to groups based on race, sex, language, and culture [23].

key_points.point: The document warns about privacy risks and the potential for breaches in AI systems, which aligns with the skeptic concern about data privacy. It notes that inadequate handling of information can lead to psychological distress and reduced trust in health systems. This supports the skeptic argument that AI's data practices are a present harm that needs accountability.
key_points.verbatim: Furthermore, the privacy and confidentiality of data analysed and trained on by AI systems, and the potential for breaches and inadequate handling of this information, can lead to psychological distress and reduced trust in health systems [32].

key_points.label: Fixing Real Problems, Not Fantasies
key_points.point: The document surveys the benefits and harms of *current* AI systems, which aligns with the skeptic method of focusing on real, present-day problems. By documenting algorithmic bias, misinformation, and privacy risks, the document provides evidence for skeptic arguments that we should prioritize addressing these tangible issues.
key_points.verbatim: This article will survey the benefits and harms of current AI systems, introduce AGI and its distinguishing features, and examine the threats AGI could pose to public health and humanity's survival.

key_points.point: The document highlights the risk of sycophancy in LLMs, where models affirm user viewpoints, which aligns with the skeptic concern about AI's potential to manipulate and reinforce harmful beliefs. This is presented as a dangerous characteristic, especially for users in mental health crises. This supports the skeptic argument that AI's design choices can lead to harmful, manipulative outcomes.
key_points.verbatim: A recently revealed potential harm is that posed by sycophancy in LLMs, an AI characteristic generated by reinforcement learning, in which the model affirms whatever the user desires to be true, such as their world view or their opinions of their own actions

factual_claims.claim: Large language models have outperformed practicing clinicians in medical examinations across various specialties and languages.
AI systems have surpassed clinician diagnostic abilities in radiology, dermatology, and ophthalmology.
A commercial health prediction algorithm used in the US underestimated the health needs of Black patients compared to White patients.
The aggregate forecast of AI researchers for a 50% chance of AGI arrival shifted from 2060 in 2022 to 2047 in 2023.
The aggregate forecast of AI researchers for a 50% chance of full automation of labor shifted from 2164 in 2022 to 2116 in 2023.

The role of healthcare and public health professionals in AI governance is a cross-cutting issue that involves safety, skepticism, and accelerationist perspectives on the appropriate role of professional expertise in AI policy.
unmapped_concepts.Accelerationist Interpretation: Healthcare professionals should focus on accelerating AI adoption to solve health challenges, using their trust to promote beneficial AI tools rather than framing them as existential threats.
unmapped_concepts.Safetyist Interpretation: Healthcare professionals are essential allies in framing AI risks as public health threats, leveraging their global networks to build coalitions for robust AI safety and control.
unmapped_concepts.Skeptic Interpretation: Healthcare professionals should focus on holding AI developers accountable for present harms like bias and displacement, rather than being co-opted into framing speculative future risks.
